You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

Based on the context, would an owner of a business owning less than 10% of an insurance company regulated by the state of New Jersey be considered a legal entity customer and/or be required to report the identity of the beneficial owner? 

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

1	Under the Beneficial Ownership Rule,
     2	1 a bank must establish and maintain written procedures
     3	that are reasonably designed to identify and verify beneficial owner(s) of legal entity
     4	customers and to include such procedures in its anti-money laundering compliance program.
     5	Legal entities, whether domestic or foreign, can be used to facilitate money laundering and
     6	other crimes because their true ownership can be concealed. The collection of beneficial
     7	ownership information by banks about legal entity customers can provide law enforcement
     8	with key details about suspected criminals who use legal entity structures to conceal their
     9	illicit activity and assets. Requiring legal entity customers seeking access to banks to disclose
    10	identifying information, such as the name, date of birth, and Social Security number of natural
    11	persons who own or control them will make such entities more transparent, and thus less
    12	attractive to criminals and those who assist them.
    13	Similar to other customer information that a bank may gather, beneficial ownership
    14	information collected under the rule may be relevant to other regulatory requirements. These
    15	other regulatory requirements include, but are not limited to, identifying suspicious activity,
    16	and determining Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned parties. Banks should
    17	define in their policies, procedures, and processes how beneficial ownership information will
    18	be used to meet other regulatory requirements.
    19	Legal Entity Customers
    20	For the purposes of the Beneficial Ownership Rule,
    21	2 a legal entity customer is defined as a
    22	corporation, limited liability company, or other entity that is created by the filing of a public
    23	document with a Secretary of State or other similar office, a general partnership, and any
    24	similar entity formed under the laws of a foreign jurisdiction that opens an account. A
    25	number of types of business entities are excluded from the definition of legal entity customer
    26	under the Beneficial Ownership rule. In addition, and subject to certain limitations, banks are
    27	not required to identify and verify the identity of the beneficial owner(s) of a legal entity
    28	customer when the customer opens certain types of accounts. For further information on
    29	exclusions and exemptions to the Beneficial Ownership Rule, see Appendix 1. These
    30	exclusions and exemptions do not alter or supersede other existing requirements related to
    31	BSA/AML and OFAC sanctions.
    32	Beneficial Owner(s)
    33	Beneficial ownership is determined under both a control prong and an ownership prong.
    34	Under the control prong, the beneficial owner is a single individual with significant responsibility
    35	to control, manage or direct a legal entity customer.3 This includes, an
    36	executive officer or senior manager (Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer, Chief
    37	Operating Officer, President), or any other individual who regularly performs similar
    38	functions. One beneficial owner must be identified under the control prong for each legal
    39	entity customer.
    40	Under the ownership prong, a beneficial owner is each individual, if any, who, directly or
    41	indirectly, through any contract, arrangement, understanding, relationship or otherwise, owns
    42	25 percent or more of the equity interests of a legal entity customer.4 If a trust owns directly
    43	or indirectly, through any contract, arrangement, understanding, relationship or otherwise, 25
    44	percent or more of the equity interests of a legal entity customer, the beneficial owner is the
    45	trustee.5
    46	 Identification of a beneficial owner under the ownership prong is not required if no
    47	individual owns 25 percent or more of a legal entity customer. Therefore, all legal entity
    48	customers will have a total of between one and five beneficial owner(s) – one individual under
    49	the control prong and zero to four individuals under the ownership prong.
    50	Exclusions from the definition of Legal Entity Customer
    51	Under 31 CFR 1010.230(e)(2) a legal entity customer does not include:
    52	• A financial institution regulated by a federal functional regulator14 or a bank regulated
    53	by a state bank regulator;
    54	• A person described in 31 CFR 1020.315(b)(2) through (5):
    55	o A department or agency of the United States, of any state, or of any political
    56	subdivision of any State;
    57	o Any entity established under the laws of the United States, of any state, or of any
    58	political subdivision of any state, or under an interstate compact between two or
    59	more states, that exercises governmental authority on behalf of the United States
    60	or any such state or political subdivision;
    61	o Any entity (other than a bank) whose common stock or analogous equity interests
    62	are listed on the New York Stock Exchange or the American Stock Exchange
    63	(currently known as the NYSE American) or have been designated as a NASDAQ
    64	National Market Security listed on the NASDAQ stock exchange (with some
    65	exceptions);
    66	o Any subsidiary (other than a bank) of any “listed entity” that is organized under
    67	the laws of the United States or of any state and at least 51 percent of whose
    68	common stock or analogous equity interest is owned by the listed entity, provided
    69	that a person that is a financial institution, other than a bank, is an exempt person
    70	only to the extent of its domestic operations;
    71	• An issuer of a class of securities registered under section 12 of the Securities
    72	Exchange Act of 1934 or that is required to file reports under section 15(d) of that Act;
    73	• An investment company, investment adviser, an exchange or clearing agency, or any
    74	other entity that is registered with the SEC;
    75	• A registered entity, commodity pool operator, commodity trading advisor, retail
    76	foreign exchange dealer, swap dealer, or major swap participant that is registered with
    77	the CFTC;
    78	• A public accounting firm registered under section 102 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act;
    79	• A bank holding company or savings and loan holding company;
    80	• A pooled investment vehicle that is operated or advised by a financial institution that
    81	is excluded under paragraph (e)(2);
    82	• An insurance company that is regulated by a state;

Based on `doc.txt`, the answer is **no** on both counts.

**1. The insurance company is not a legal entity customer.**
The document defines a legal entity customer as "a corporation, limited liability company, or other entity that is created by the filing of a public document with a Secretary of State or other similar office, a general partnership, and any similar entity formed under the laws of a foreign jurisdiction that opens an account" (doc.txt). However, it lists exclusions, and among them is "An insurance company that is regulated by a state" (doc.txt). Since the insurance company in question is regulated by the state of New Jersey, it falls within this exclusion and is not a legal entity customer.

**2. An owner of less than 10% would not be a reportable beneficial owner under the ownership prong.**
Even setting aside the exclusion, the ownership prong only captures owners at a 25% threshold: "Under the ownership prong, a beneficial owner is each individual, if any, who, directly or indirectly, through any contract, arrangement, understanding, relationship or otherwise, owns 25 percent or more of the equity interests of a legal entity customer" (doc.txt). An owner holding less than 10% is below that threshold, so "Identification of a beneficial owner under the ownership prong is not required if no individual owns 25 percent or more of a legal entity customer" (doc.txt).

**Note on scope:** The document does not specifically name New Jersey; it applies the exclusion to any "insurance company that is regulated by a state." It also does not address the individual "owner of a business" as a separate category — the rule's obligations attach to the entity that opens the account (the legal entity customer), not to a natural-person owner standing alone.
